preamble: Deaffrication of the postalveolar ejective affricate [tʃʼ] to the alveolo-palatal ejective fricative [ɕʼ] in Kabardian (East Circassian). In words where Adyghe (West Circassian) кӏ [tʃʼ] continues Proto-Circassian *tʃʼ, literary Kabardian has щӏ [ɕʼ]: Adyghe кӏэ [t͡ʃʼa] 'new' corresponds to Kabardian щӏэ [ɕʼa]. Wiktionary reconstructs Proto-Circassian *t͡ʃʼa 'new' and *pt͡ʃʼəħ 'dream' with the affricate. Nikolayev & Starostin (1994: 199) list two Proto-Adyghe-Kabardian glottalized affricates, *č̣ and *č̣́, that stay affricates in Bzhedug and Temirgoy Adyghe but both appear as ṣ́ in Kabardian. The related West Caucasian languages also have an affricate here: Starling gives Abkhaz a-č̣á and Abaza č̣a 'young, fresh' and Ubykh č̣a 'good' beside Proto-Adyghe-Kabardian *č̣́a 'new', and notes that Ubykh č̣ regularly corresponds to Circassian č̣́. Wikipedia's Proto-Circassian article calls the change spirantization, lists the East Circassian Besleney dialect as unaffected, and has the retroflex *t͡ʂʼ (Adyghe чӏ) merge into the same ɕʼ, as in Adyghe гъучӏы : Kabardian гъущӏ 'iron' (Starling ʁʷǝč̣ǝ : ʁʷǝṣ́); that branch is not covered here because the atlas has no symbol for [ʈʂʼ]. Kabardian ɕʼ also has a source that is not [tʃʼ]: for the 'ten' set (Adyghe пшӀы : Kabardian пщӀы, both written ṗṣ́ǝ by Starling), Kuipers, as reported by Nikolayev & Starostin (1994: 197), reconstructs a glottalized fricative, and Nikolayev & Starostin themselves a glottalized hissing-hushing affricate *ć̣ that became a fricative in both languages. Kabardian кӏэ 'tail', from Proto-Circassian *kʲʼa (Wiktionary), did not take part.
